stemMd:
In the early 1800s, the river town of Haldmere was known for its rope, which local workshops twisted from hemp grown on nearby farms. By the 1830s, however, most of the rope sold in Haldmere was imported from coastal cities, and only two of the town's eleven rope workshops remained open. Historian Ondine Ray claims that this shift was caused mainly by the opening of the Haldmere Canal in 1824, which made it far cheaper to bring goods into the town.

Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ray's claim?

options.label: A
options.textMd: After the canal opened, farmers near Haldmere began shipping most of their grain to coastal cities by barge instead of selling it in the town's market.

options.label: B
options.textMd: Sailors of the period considered rope twisted from Haldmere hemp to be stronger and longer-lasting than most of the rope made in the coastal cities.

options.label: C
options.textMd: Merchants' records show that imported rope in Haldmere fell to half its former price within three years of the canal opening, while local rope sales declined.

options.label: D
options.textMd: Letters written by Haldmere rope makers in the 1810s complain that disease had ruined several of the region's hemp harvests in a row.

explanationMd:
Start by naming the exact link the claim makes: the canal made bringing goods in cheaper, and that is why imported rope replaced local rope. Supporting evidence should connect the canal to cheaper imported rope and connect cheaper imported rope to the decline of local rope.

The merchants' records do both: imported rope halved in price right after the canal opened, and local rope sales fell over the same period. The timing and the direction of both changes are what Ray's claim predicts.

Check the others by asking whether each bears on the canal-to-price link at all. Diseased hemp harvests would point to a different cause; grain shipments concern goods leaving the town, not rope coming in; and a reputation for stronger local rope, if anything, makes the shift harder to explain.

distractorRationale.d: This offers a rival cause for the decline of local rope making (poor hemp harvests), and it dates from before the canal opened, so it would weaken rather than support the claim that the canal was the main cause.
distractorRationale.a: This shows the canal changed trade in Haldmere, but in grain moving out of the town. Ray's claim is about cheaper rope coming in, which this finding does not address.
distractorRationale.b: A preference for local rope says nothing about the canal or about prices. If anything, it makes the switch to imported rope harder to explain, so it does not support Ray's account.

accessibilityText: A short history passage. In the early 1800s the river town of Haldmere was known for rope that local workshops twisted from nearby hemp. By the 1830s most rope sold there was imported from coastal cities, and only two of eleven rope workshops remained. Historian Ondine Ray claims the shift was caused mainly by the opening of the Haldmere Canal in 1824, which made it far cheaper to bring goods into the town. The question asks which finding would most directly support Ray's claim. The choices are: after the canal opened, nearby farmers began shipping most of their grain to coastal cities by barge instead of selling it in the town's market; sailors considered Haldmere rope stronger and longer-lasting than most rope made in the coastal cities; merchants' records show that imported rope fell to half its former price within three years of the canal opening, while local rope sales declined; and letters from Haldmere rope makers in the 1810s complain that disease ruined several hemp harvests in a row.

provenance.notes: Original command-of-evidence item. Haldmere, its canal, its rope trade and Ray's claim are invented; the key matches both links in the causal claim.
